Antes de las redes neuronales, y todavía: Before neural networks, and still today in a great many places, the answer to “what is this?” is given by looking at what it resembles. Resembling is being close, and being close is a distance. Reducing a photo to sixteen colours is also k-means, over the pixels seen as points of the colour space. And nearest neighbours is still the first choice in recommendation systems by similarity, in identifying species from measurements and as a benchmark to compare against: if a complicated model cannot beat nearest neighbours, that model is redundant.

Los vecinos más cercanos los describiero: Nearest neighbours was described by Evelyn Fix and Joseph Hodges in 1951, in a technical report for the US air force that never came out as a paper; the theoretical result that made them respectable is due to Thomas Cover and Peter Hart, in 1967, and it says something remarkable: with a great deal of data, the nearest-neighbour method is wrong at most twice as often as the best possible classifier. The $k$-means algorithm was proposed by Stuart Lloyd at Bell Labs in 1957, though it was not published until 1982, and the name was given by James MacQueen in 1967.

It reads: “d of a, b, is the square root of a one minus b one squared, plus a two minus b two squared, plus…”.

It is Pythagoras' theorem, with as many summands as the data have columns. With two, it is the usual distance in the plane; with five hundred, the formula is the same even though it can no longer be drawn.

To compare distances the square root is not needed: if $d_1 < d_2$, then also $d_1^2 < d_2^2$. That is why programs usually work with the square and save a square root on every comparison.
Se lee: <em>«jota es el sumatorio, sobre:
It reads: “J is the sum, over the points, of the squared norm of x sub i minus c sub a of i”, where $a(i)$ is the centre point $i$ is assigned to.

It is the sum of the squared distances from each point to its centre. Assigning each point to the nearest centre can only lower it, because each point moves to a smaller summand. And relocating the centre at the mean does too, because [[pe-descriptiva|the mean]] is precisely the point that minimises the sum of squared distances to a set. Since it always goes down and cannot go down for ever, the process terminates.
